headline: The supported Node version is now 24.21.0
summary: `engines.node` rises from `>=24.19.0` to `>=24.21.0`, the current patch level of the active LTS line. 24.21.0 carries OpenSSL 3.5.8 and the NSS 3.126 root store, both of which the framework's TLS paths read directly. Operators on 24.19.x or 24.20.x should upgrade Node before taking this release. npm treats `engines` as advisory unless `engine-strict` is set, so an install on a lower version prints a warning and then completes, leaving the framework running on a runtime it does not support. Set `engine-strict=true` to have the mismatch refused instead.

items.title: `engines.node` requires 24.21.0
items.body:
The floor moves to Node 24.21.0. It ships OpenSSL 3.5.8 and updates the bundled root certificates to NSS 3.126, so the trust store behind outbound TLS, certificate validation and the mail transports comes from that release. It also corrects a crash in `dns.setServers()` when a resolver is given port 0, tightens port-range validation in the same call, and stops `dgram` discarding bind errors when a callback is supplied.

The framework's own behaviour is unchanged by those three. `b.network.dns.setServers()` already refuses a resolver port outside [1,65535], including 0, before the call reaches Node, and the framework's UDP sockets bind implicitly and attach an error listener rather than passing a bind callback. The floor moves for the OpenSSL and root-store updates.

CI, the publish workflow and the release-container workflow now install 24.21.0, and the README and SECURITY.md requirement lines state it.

items.title: `b.codepointClass.decodeEntityAt`, `decodeNamedEntityAt` and `isUrlSchemeStrippable`
items.body: `decodeEntityAt(s, at)` decodes the one numeric or named entity reference that begins at index `at` of `s` and returns `{ text, next }`, or `null` when no reference begins there. `decodeNamedEntityAt(s, at)` does the same for a named reference only, returning `null` for a numeric one. `decodeMarkupEntities` decodes numeric references in one pass and named references in a second pass over the result, so a numeric reference that yields an ampersand can complete a named reference with the text after it; a caller walking by position reproduces that order by decoding the numeric reference and then offering the ampersand it produced, with the following text, to `decodeNamedEntityAt`. `isUrlSchemeStrippable(cp)` reports whether a code point is one that URL-scheme normalization removes: a C0 control or space, tab, line feed, carriage return, or a zero-width character. Together they let a scheme be located by position in a document without copying or normalizing the whole of it, which is how `b.guardMarkdown` now reads link destinations.

items.title: An `xn--` label with no Punycode payload is refused on every runtime
items.body:
`b.safeUrl`, `b.mail.toAscii()` and `b.publicSuffix` read the runtime's URL machinery as a verdict on whether a host is well-formed. It maps rather than validates, and its answer for a payload-less ACE label moved between Node releases. On 24.21.0 `url.domainToASCII("xn--")` returns `"xn--"` unchanged and `new URL("https://xn--/")` is accepted with hostname `xn--`; on 26 the first returns the empty string and the second throws.

The effect was that the same input was accepted on one runtime and refused on the other. On 24.21.0 `b.mail.toAscii("xn--")` returned `"xn--"`, `b.publicSuffix` accepted it as a real domain after it passed the letter-digit-hyphen check, and `b.safeUrl.format("https://xn--/")` returned the URL instead of throwing. An operator's host validation depended on which Node they were running.

The framework now decides this itself. An `xn--` label must carry a payload that decodes to something other than itself, which refuses `xn--`, `xn--a`, `xn--zz` and `xn--.de` while leaving every well-formed A-label untouched. `b.mail.toAscii()` returns `null`, `b.publicSuffix` throws `public-suffix/invalid-domain`, and `b.safeUrl.parse()` and `b.safeUrl.format()` throw a typed `SafeUrlError`, identically on 24.21.0 and 26. The rule has one implementation, the new `b.guardDomain.aceLabelsCarryPayload()`. `b.guardDomain.validate()` and `.sanitize()` apply it too, under every profile: the guard already refused a bare `xn--` at high severity, and now reports `domain.punycode-undecodable` for a payload that decodes to nothing, so `xn--a.example.com` is refused where it was previously accepted at the balanced and permissive profiles. A well-formed A-label is unaffected, and the profile that refuses A-labels outright still does.

The guard also reads the label separators UTS 46 recognizes. It split on the ASCII dot alone, so a name written with the ideographic or fullwidth stop (`example。xn--a.com`) presented as a single label and every per-label rule was skipped for what followed the separator. All four separators normalize to the ASCII one before any rule runs, which is what keeps the whole-domain rules working too: `127。0。0。1` and `foo。localhost` are refused as the IP literal and special-use name they resolve to, and a trailing separator is the fully-qualified marker in whichever spelling it arrives.

Hosts reached through the other URL entry points are unaffected: the origin and host comparisons in CSRF protection, the SSRF guard and the WebSocket origin check match against expected values, so a malformed host fails them on both runtimes.

This was found by the release's own Node bump. The container leg runs the pinned floor, and two tests that pass on 26 failed on 24.21.0.

items.title: Two marker reasons in `lib/` ended mid-sentence
items.body: `lib/network-tls.js` and `lib/pqc-agent.js` each carry a suppression marker whose reason is the prose a reader weighs when re-checking why the exemption holds. Both ended on a dangling word, so neither stated its reason. The TLS one now records that the ECH feature probe's lookup aborts, so it negotiates nothing and has no posture to apply; the certificate one records that the context it builds is discarded and never serves a handshake.

items.title: A marker reason named a primitive that does not carry the pattern
items.body: The ISO-8601 instant literal is shared by three primitives. The reasons in `lib/ai-model-manifest.js` and `lib/metrics.js` named `mail-server-imap` as the third, which does not carry it. The three are `ai-model-manifest`, `metrics` text-render and `content-credentials`, and `lib/content-credentials.js` carried the literal with no reason at all. All three now state the same reason, and it is the operative one: none of the three imports `safe-schema`, whose `DATETIME_RE` also admits a numeric offset, so sharing that would pull a validation module into a hot-path sink for a 50-byte literal.

items.title: `b.guardMarkdown` inspects the destination of a link whose label contains brackets
items.body:
The inline-link scanner and the reference-definition scanner each took the first `]` as the end of a label. A label may contain balanced brackets, and a backslash escapes the character after it, so a linked image such as `[![alt](img.png)](javascript:...)`, a label with an inner bracketed run such as `[a [b] c](javascript:...)`, or an escaped bracket such as `[a\]b](javascript:...)` closed the label early. The outer destination was never extracted, the scheme policy never saw it, `validate()` reported no issue, and `sanitize()` returned the input unchanged, so a CommonMark renderer downstream produced a live link to the uninspected destination. Both scanners now honor nesting and escapes, and each of those shapes is refused under every profile. A benign nested or escaped label is unaffected. Brackets inside a code span take no part in matching, as in CommonMark, so a backtick-quoted bracket can neither close a label early nor turn an image into a plain link that escapes the image cap. Code spans are paired exactly as CommonMark pairs them: a backtick run opens a span only when a later run of the same length closes it, the earliest opener that finds a closer wins over any pair inside it, a run with no closer is literal text, and an escaped backtick cannot open a span but does close one, as in cmark, whose closer scan is raw. So a stray backtick in a label does not hide the link after it, and an inner pair inside a longer span does not leave the longer span unapplied. An autolink and a raw HTML tag bind tighter than a link too, so a bracket inside `<https://example.com/[>`, inside a tag attribute, or inside an HTML comment is literal as well, and the first of these constructs in text order wins: a backtick inside an autolink is literal, and an autolink inside a code span is literal. A code span binds tighter than a link in CommonMark, but a link-first renderer reads a backtick inside a destination as part of the URL, so a construct fabricated from that backtick would hide the hostile link after it; links and reference definitions are therefore extracted both with and without these constructs whenever one of them contains a bracket, and every match found either way is inspected. A link label and a code span may contain a line ending, and a blank line ends both, so `[x\ny](javascript:...)` is now extracted and refused where no earlier version extracted it. The pairing is one reverse pass and one forward pass over the backtick runs, and two further growth checks hold a document of back-to-back code spans, and code spans after thousands of unmatched run lengths, linear.

Verifying the report exposed a second gap in the same gate. `dangerousSchemePolicy`, `imageSchemePolicy`, `referenceLinkPolicy` and `autolinkSchemePolicy` grade the severity of a dangerous scheme in an inline link, an image, a reference definition or an autolink, and a value of `allow` also skipped the check entirely, so at the permissive profile `[ref]: javascript:...` and `<javascript:...>` passed with no issue. Each policy still sets the severity; a dangerous scheme is reported under every value, so `allow` now means not critical rather than not inspected.

Matching brackets correctly also exposed two quadratic paths. Nested labels close at decreasing offsets, so every link's destination is a suffix of the one before it. The extractor copied each label and each destination for every link, and the scheme check normalized each overlapping destination in full, so a 32 KB document of nested brackets took 1.3 seconds to validate at the permissive profile and 6.7 seconds at 64 KB. With entity-encoded control padding as the shared suffix the normalizing path could not be skipped, and 56 KB took 2.7 seconds. Bounding the inspected bytes would have been a bypass, since normalization strips unbounded leading control padding the way a browser does.

Label and destination text are no longer copied during validation; bracket mates are found in one pass and looked up; extraction stops once the link and image caps are exceeded; a destination whose first bytes are all printable ASCII with no entity reference or percent escape is classified from that prefix alone, since normalization would not change it; and otherwise the scheme is read by position through a memoized index of the next character that survives normalization, so shared padding is walked once for every link that starts inside it. Reading by position recognizes the same references the whole-string decoder does, in its order: numeric references are decoded first, and a named reference is then recognized even where its ampersand, its letters or its closing semicolon were written numerically, so `javascript&colon;alert(1)` and `javascript&colon;alert(1)` are both read as `javascript:`, while an ampersand a named reference produced does not begin a further one, so `javascript&colon;alert(1)` is not. A space inside a destination is kept, since normalization trims space only at the ends, so `java script:` is a relative path and not a scheme, while any amount of whitespace between a scheme name and its colon is passed over, as the scheme reader has always done, so a long run of encoded spaces there does not push the colon out of view. Each of these verdicts is asserted against the whole-string normalization rather than against a fixed expectation. The 64 KB document now validates in about 38 ms and the padded 56 KB one in about 61 ms. Three growth checks hold the scan linear at the permissive profile, whose caps do not truncate the input, for unmatched openers, nested destinations, and entity-padded overlap.

The indexes behind this hold one entry per run of characters actually walked rather than one per character or one per document position, so a document with no links allocates none of them and a single 4 MiB destination costs about 4 MiB. The bracket index is built once for links and reference definitions together, and it is bounded: a document with more than 65536 opening brackets is refused with `markdown.delimiter-cap` before any index is built, so a document of brackets alone can neither exhaust the heap nor smuggle a link through an unindexed scan as a clean verdict.

Reported by Dicky Mulia Fiqri (@dickymuliafiqri).

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.7.8
items.body:
`lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carries 0.7.8, refreshed through `scripts/vendor-update.sh` with the `MANIFEST.json` SHA-256 hashes regenerated alongside it. 0.7.3 applies the read-options-once shape to timestamp verification, so every pass there reads one answer.

It fixes an iteration-cap bypass in `pki.pkcs12.open` and `pki.pkcs12.verifyMac`. `opts.maxIterations` is the caller's bound on key-derivation work, and it was re-read by each pass that applied it. An option reached through an accessor answers each read separately, so one returning a valid integer to the shape check and a non-numeric value later left the cap as `NaN`, and no count is above `NaN`, so the comparison stopped refusing anything. Both verbs now read the options object once at entry. A caller passing plain values was never affected.

It fixes a name-constraint bypass in `pki.path.validate`. An excluded subtree states the names a certificate must not present, and a wildcard `dNSName` stands for every name one label below its parent rather than for the literal text. Comparing the text alone let a leaf carrying only `*.example.com` pass an exclusion of `bar.example.com`, a name that leaf does present. Any chain whose certificate authority relies on an excluded `dNSName` subtree to keep a subordinate away from a name was affected. The permitted direction is unchanged.

It also fixes a verification flaw in `pki.sigstore.verifyBundle`. A bundle supplied as an object had its fields read more than once, and a field that answered differently across those reads let one transparency-log body be bound to the signature while a different one was proven, so a signature the log never recorded could be attested by an authentic entry for something else and still verify. A bundle supplied as JSON text was never affected. The same release holds an object bundle to being plain data: an accessor field is refused rather than called, and the size and depth limits that bound the text route now bound the object route under the same numbers.

It also adds RFC 8879 zstd certificate compression to `pki.tls`, which is available on this release's Node floor. Each algorithm is offered only where the running Node faults on a truncated frame rather than returning the prefix, and 24.21.0 does.

items.title: Vendored data files refreshed
items.body: The Public Suffix List and the SecLists common-password corpus are refreshed to their 2026-09-08 upstream state and re-signed. `b.publicSuffix` and the password-strength checks read the newer data; no API changes.

items.title: CI cannot drift off the supported Node version
items.body: The Node floor is written out in the workflow pins and again in the step names beside them, and nothing held those to `engines.node`. Raising the floor without them would test the framework on a runtime it no longer supports, and publish from one, with nothing reporting the gap. A new check compares every pinned `node-version` and every `Set up Node <version>` label against the floor. A bare major such as `'24'` resolves to the newest of that line and is left alone.

items.title: The marker checks now read the file that defines the markers
items.body: The check that every `// allow:<class>` marker names a registered class skipped `codebase-patterns.test.js` entirely, on the stated grounds that the file holds the class registry and the regexes naming classes. It reads only the `//` comment portion of a line, and both of those live in code, so neither was ever in scope. The file is the largest in the repository, and the skip had hidden four stale mentions: a placeholder written in marker syntax, and two names that a rename retired, `dynamic-require` and `seal-without-aad`. All four are corrected and the file is now scanned.

items.title: A rule left on a retired class name is reported again
items.body: When a suppression class is renamed, the old name is recorded as retired so that every rule and marker using it has to be re-verified rather than silently keeping the old exemption. The check that compares the registry against the rules returned early on a retired name, and the check that hunts retired names does not read the file the rules live in, so a rule left on an old name after a rename was reported by neither. It is now reported, naming the token and its rename. No rule was using one.

items.title: Comment prose can no longer drift into a suppression marker
items.body: A marker is honored when it appears anywhere on the offending line or the line above it. Line-wrapping a sentence that names a class can therefore land that name at the start of a comment line, directly above scanned code, where nothing distinguishes it from a deliberate exemption. One such line sat above a scan call and named a class that had been retired months earlier. A second wrap split a class name across a line break, so the marker a reader copies out of the documentation named no detector. A new check reports both shapes. It does not require markers to sit at the start of a comment, because many legitimate ones follow a sentence within one.
